# Posālamāṇavapucchā (Snp 5.15 (PTS Snp 215))

**ID:** Snp 5.15 (PTS Snp 215)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Posālamāṇavapucchā
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Posālamāṇavapucchā* ("The Questions of the Student Posala") is the fourteenth dialogue in the *Pārāyanavagga* of the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 5.15, PTS Snp 215, verse 1112) [Norman 1997-2001; Saddhatissa 2013; Hazra 1994]. It is a short dialogue consisting of four verses that form a single question and answer [Wynne, Origin of Buddhist Meditation]. Unlike earlier portions of the collection such as the *Upasīvamāṇavapucchā*, which are composed in Triṣṭubh, the *Posālamāṇavapucchā* is composed in the Śloka metre [Wynne, Origin of Buddhist Meditation].

The text focuses on how to develop insight and achieve liberation after mastering the meditative perception or state of nothingness (*ākiñcañña*) [Wynne 2007; Wynne, Origin of Buddhist Meditation]. While the *Upasīvamāṇavapucchā* instructs the practitioner to mindfully observe nothingness without delineating how that meditative practice leads to release, the *Posālamāṇavapucchā* functions as a continuation that expands on this doctrine by explaining how liberation is attained from the state of nothingness [Wynne 2007; Wynne, Origin of Buddhist Meditation]. Alongside the dialogues with Upasīva and Udaya, it forms a crucial group of texts for understanding early Buddhist meditation and its engagement with Brahminic meditative practices [Wynne 2007; Wynne, Origin of Buddhist Meditation].

In the canonical commentary tradition, the text is treated in the *Cullaniddesa* under the *Posālamāṇavapucchāniddesa* (Cnd 18) and the *Pucchā* (Cnd 2) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus records substantial Pali-internal text reuse with both chapters, notably sharing segments 2.1–3.5 with Cnd 18 (§18.5–20.5, similarity 0.98) and segments 0.2–4.7 with Cnd 2 (§81.0–85.0, similarity 0.99) [DharmaNexus]. Beyond Pali literature, DharmaNexus automatically aligns the dialogue with Harivarman's *Satyasiddhiśāstra* (*Tattvasiddhiśāstra*), identifying four matches with scores up to 85 [DharmaNexus].
